content.title: About
content.content: Spaghetti squash is a variety of winter squash whose flesh separates into strands that resemble spaghetti when cooked. Boiling, baking, or steaming softens the flesh, creating long, noodle‑like fibers with a mild, slightly sweet flavor and very low calorie content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the pasta‑like texture of the cooked fruit.
It belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family and is native to North America.
Raw fruits can weigh 1–3 kg, but lose about half their weight after cooking.
The seeds are edible after roasting and are a good source of healthy fats.
Spaghetti squash is popular in low‑carb and gluten‑free diets as a pasta substitute.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One hundred grams of cooked spaghetti squash provides roughly 20 kcal, making it ideal for weight management.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and niacin, which are important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Rich in carotenoids (beta‑carotene) and vitamin C, which combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides potassium, magnesium, and manganese, essential for blood pressure regulation, muscle function, and metabolism.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Although uncommon, some individuals may be allergic to cucurbit vegetables.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Raw seeds and skin contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation if consumed in excess.

items.title: Overeating
items.content: Large portions may cause gastrointestinal discomfort due to the high fiber content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked spaghetti squash can be served as a pasta alternative with tomato sauce, pesto, vegetable ragù, or in casseroles. It also works well in salads, soups, and Asian‑style noodle dishes. Drizzle with olive oil and season with salt, pepper, or herbs before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw squash in a cool, dry place for up to 2–3 weeks. After cooking, keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. Freeze cooked strands in freezer bags for longer storage (up to 3 months).
